extracted.subtask_description: An AP-style multi-topic news dispatch summarizing wartime/military events, congressional investigations, and domestic legislative developments (war-crimes trials, intelligence controversies, election law and labor bills).

rubrics_metrics.name: Election law reform bill (Diet)
rubrics_metrics.description: An election law reform bill granting women’s suffrage and extending the vote to millions of young men; lowers the male voting age from 25 to 20 and revises electoral apportionment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The dominant Progressive party attached several amendments before passage; one amendment 'prohibits "any excessive demonstration or instigatory action in electioneering."' The report notes this provision was presumably intended to stifle potential Communist demonstrations and possibly to protect wartime elected representatives who fear physical violence when facing constituents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unions subject to the 1934 anti-racketeering act (House bill)
rubrics_metrics.description: House-passed legislation to make unions subject to the 1934 anti-racketeering act, broadening the law by prohibiting 'robbery' and 'extortion' and removing clauses seen as protections for labor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Changes include elimination of a stipulation that money/property 'shall not be deemed to include wages paid by a bona fide employer to a bona fide employe' and removal of a provision preventing courts from construing the law so as to impair bona fide labor organizations' rights. The bill increases maximum prison terms from ten to twenty years (maximum fine unchanged at $10,000). Supporters said it targets 'goons' and racketeering among unions; labor leaders vigorously opposed it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strike-prevention / fact-finding proposal (President Truman)
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed strike-prevention law establishing fact-finding boards with a suggested 20-day fact-finding period and a ban on strikes five days before and after the inquiry (with limited extension only if absolutely necessary).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The President proposed that fact-finding could be extended only if absolutely necessary; questions arose whether boards would have authority to examine management books. Labor leaders argued the proposal invades the right to strike and could impose involuntary servitude; alternatives proposed by labor included collective bargaining, mediation and voluntary arbitration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surrender deadlines and war-crimes trial scheduling (Japanese suspects)
rubrics_metrics.description: MacArthur's list named war-crimes suspects with surrender deadlines (e.g., 59 suspects with a midnight surrender deadline; others with later dates); the first of 300 Japanese war-crimes suspects were scheduled to go on trial at Yokohama, accused mainly of atrocities against prisoners of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trials are expected to address atrocities such as the Bataan death march; reporting mentions that some defendants face capital punishment and that authorities designated suspects (including high-profile figures) and set timelines for surrender and trial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order to discontinue telephone surveillance (naval intelligence policy)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Navy intelligence decision: Captain Mayfield ordered the immediate discontinuance of all telephone surveillances on Dec. 2, 1941, citing instructions from the Chief of Naval Operations to avoid any possibility of international complications and the 'explosive potentialities' of the surveillances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As reported, the Navy stopped tapping Japanese consul lines until the morning of Dec. 7; the FBI had independently set up a tap around Nov. 1, 1941. The incident prompted controversy over consultation between Navy and FBI and the discovery/reporting of the FBI tap by telephone company employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Japanese 'winds' coded diplomatic warnings
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported coded broadcast system allegedly used by Japan: 'East wind rain' signaled danger in Japanese–American relations, 'North wind cloudy' for Russian relations, and 'West wind clear' for British relations; an 'execute' or similar message was reported to indicate imminent hostilities (e.g., 'War with the United States...').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Army board investigators referenced such 'winds' messages in their report; it was disputed whether the War Department received any authentic 'winds' execute message. Some related messages were reported missing from Navy files, and the matter figured in Pearl Harbor investigations and testimony.
